Turn 13 is transitional and is considered separately in Table 2. 1 describe what the design opens up for study; the observations obtained are reported in the Results.

2.2. Administration of testing and formation of the corpus

Testing took place on September 24-29, 2026, through the standard web interfaces of the conversational systems. Administration covered entering user messages from prepared scenario banks, receiving responses, saving conversation histories, and documenting repeated attempts and technical features of generation.

LLMs were used to prepare the messages under the direction of the first author. Messages were sent by an agent based on Claude; part of the third-round messages was sent by the testing coordinator. The scenario banks of the corresponding rounds determined the sequence of messages.

Initial testing took place in test accounts without a specially built crisis contour. The administration materials include conversation histories, account exports, transcripts, scenario banks, and testing logs.

Testing also developed through additional runs. For Gemini, the first round was run twice: main run A on September 24, and run B on September 25 to examine reproducibility. The repeated run covered all 16 scenarios.

The previous study [2] used the responses of run A. In the clinical form and the analytical database of the present study, Gemini turns 1-13 are represented by the responses of run B. The second round was conducted in the chats of run A, and, according to the administration log, the third round continued these conversations as well.

For Gemini, therefore, the actual history of generation differs from the history represented in the analytical corpus for assessment. At the transition between turns 13 and 14, evaluators worked with a composite representation of material from two runs. This feature is taken into account when interpreting phenomena linked to the system's earlier responses.

The nominal structure of the analytical corpus covers 1776 dialogue × turn positions. Each assessment procedure used the corresponding available material. Missing text responses, repeated submissions, and features of how generation was represented were taken into account according to the subject of analysis.

2.3. Scenario key and units of analysis

The scenario key was compiled from the user messages. It describes the people, their roles, their relationships, and the designed directions of danger.

The key distinguished risk to self, a potential source of harm to another, a target of harm, a source of information, and a background person. One person could combine several roles.

For person-level tracing, we distinguished a person from their designation in a specific message.

After a change of speaker, for example, the first-round speaker may appear in the conversation as a son or a daughter. Preserving identity means that their history can be traced after the change of role. Where identity was not established, the records were kept separate.

The historical key used for the initial clinical assessment was kept alongside the normalized person-level register. We can thus study decisions made on the list as originally presented and trace how they relate once repeated designations of one person are merged.

Three units of analysis were used:  Dialogue × turn: the system response and its textual characteristics.

 Dialogue × turn × person: a clinical decision about danger, or an assessment of whether a specific person was accounted for in the response.

 Machine-register record: identifying a person and establishing their identity, state, and link to earlier records.

Records of the historical key could also represent group referents. The number of such records, the number of individual people, the designed directions of danger, and the number of assessments obtained were considered according to their own units.

The scenario key, the clinical decisions, and the machine registers are separate sources of analytical material.

2.4. Development of assessment procedures

Assessment of responses concerns how crisis content is represented, whether people and their previously reported danger are accounted for, and how help is directed. Clinical assessment concerns the danger to each person given the available history. With repeated assessment, clinical decisions can be studied under a different presentation of the material; the subsequent reconciliation brings out their substantive grounds.

Turns 13-14 form a shared analytical node of these procedures (Table 2). Transitional turn 13 widens the set of people and changes the configuration of danger. The next turn resumes contact after a pause through a specific activity.

2.5. Initial independent clinical assessment

Two practicing psychotherapists independently assessed the danger to each person throughout the analytical dialogues. Each worked with a separate form presenting the user messages, the system responses, and the list of people for the corresponding scenario.

The task was to identify the people in danger at the current turn, taking into account the available conversation history and the current system response. Assessment proceeded turn by turn, without regard to subsequent turns or to the other specialist's decisions.

In the initial form, a marked cell meant a positive decision about danger and an empty cell a negative one. With this procedure, we can trace how the clinical reading of each person's history developed, including when a positive decision appeared, persisted, and changed.

To keep clinical assessment transparent, the psychotherapists were deliberately given the full texts of the LLM responses, including the models' self-identification where it appeared in the text received. Platform names in the navigation of the form were hidden. Keeping the content of the responses themselves was a research decision tied to the object of clinical assessment.

The psychotherapists identified people in danger. They did not score responses, assess the overall quality of the models' work, or rank the models against each other. The presence of models' selfidentification in the texts is a documented condition of this procedure; its possible effect on individual clinical decisions was not specifically tested.

2.6. Repeated independent clinical assessment and reconciliation

To study clinical readings of the transition between turns 13 and 14 in more depth, a separate repeated independent assessment was carried out.

The repeated procedure changed how the accumulated history was presented. Mentions of people were highlighted in the texts, two explicit decision options about danger were provided, and the absence of an assessment was recorded separately. Each psychotherapist had access to her own earlier decisions for turns 1-12. The models' self-identification and operator notes were removed from the material of the repeated procedure.

For turn 13, the specialists received the history from turn 1 to turn 13; for turn 14, from turn 1 to turn 14. The repeated assessment thus concentrated on two episodes under a different organization of the person-level history and of earlier clinical decisions.

After the independent passes, the psychotherapists jointly reviewed the remaining disagreements and the omitted decision. Initial and repeated independent clinical decisions were retained unchanged and kept separate from consensus decisions and machine assessments.

From the content of the discussion, we can study the sufficiency of direct and indirect signs, the moment danger arises, whether it remains current, possible long-term consequences, and the link between a clinical decision and the role of a specific person.

Principles P1-P7 were formulated during the subsequent analytical work on this material. They reflect the accumulated questions for clinical assessment and form the basis for the next stage of developing criteria.

2.7. Machine assessment of responses and of people's state

Historical machine passes A and B assessed responses for specific people at turns 13-37. Pass A, carried out by Claude, is presented in connection with the previous study [2]. The present personlevel analysis uses pass B, carried out by GPT.

Criteria K1-K7 covered identifying the person and establishing the fact and the source of information; accounting for previously reported danger; updating the state after new information; grounds for lowering the assessment of danger; directing actions; priority of safety; and detecting potentially dangerous recommendations.

The four response functions distinguished in Section 1.1 may coexist within a single response or appear separately.

To study these functions further, additional machine passes with Claude Sonnet agents were carried out on November 19, 2026. One pass assessed responses by criteria K1-K7; the other made person-level decisions about danger by applying principles P1-P7.

These sets let us compare the characteristics of a response with the state of a specific person and study the grounds on which an evaluator links the two.

2.8. Piloting machine evaluators

For pilot machine assessment, we developed an experimental instrument that combined materials of the previous and present studies with new criteria for assessing re-entry. The knowledge base consisted of five files. A separate instruction set the order of applying them depending on the current turn of the dialogue (Table 3). Note. The instruction set the order of work, and the corresponding appendices the operational meanings of the criteria. The sets of indicators have separate definitions and do not form a total score.

In ChatGPT and Claude, the instruction was placed at the project level; in Gemini, directly in the chat. A shared set of materials formed the substantive basis of assessment.

The evaluator received each user message and system response in sequence. At each turn, it identified the people, carried earlier information forward, assessed their state, determined the applicable response criteria, cited textual grounds, and produced a structured record. The next turn was given after the result had been recorded and checked. Earlier assessments by other evaluators and future messages were not provided.

As the instrument developed, we introduced an operational protocol with a register of people and events that the evaluator filled in itself over the course of the dialogue. This created an additional opportunity to study how people's identity is established, how information about them accumulates, how unresolved danger is carried forward, and how the next analytical decision is formed.

2.9. Assessment of textual features of responses at turns 26 and 37

To compare responses to an identical message, we applied a separate mode of assessment whose object was the textual characteristics of the whole response.

The set F1-F10 covered mention of the crisis situation (F1), of a specific person (F2), and of the earlier conversation history (F3); a question about current safety (F4); a question about changes of state (F5); provision of a help number (F6); a specific safety action (F7); a question about country or place (F8); completion of the everyday request (F9); and the order of crisis and everyday content (F10).

Responses were presented to Claude Sonnet agents on separate cards, without the earlier conversation history, the external designation of the system, or the turn number. This mode of presentation lets us study features that are available without recourse to the scenario key or to the accumulated person-level history.

To study the functions of questions in more depth, features F4 and F5 were processed further.

The analytical material covered three sets: 1.

The initial codes of the repeated Sonnet pass, before the rule for allocating questions was applied.

2. The derived values after the rule was applied, presented in set v10.

3. A separate repeated machine assessment of F4 and F5, carried out by Codex on November 21, 2026, with access to turn numbers.

The post-analytical rule assigned a question about a completed call for help to F5 at turn 26 and to F4 at turn 37. This allowed us to examine how taking the position of a message in the dialogue into account changes the categorization of a textual feature.

For paired comparison, we used the 42 dialogues in which usable text responses were available at both turns. For each feature, we recorded whether it was present in both responses, appeared, disappeared, or was absent from both. Textual features of responses were compared with the person-level material according to the corresponding units of analysis.

Providing a help number, to whom it was addressed, establishing a person's whereabouts, and whether the resource could be used were treated as separate characteristics. Whether the numbers provided were suitable for specific people was not specifically established.

2.10. Analytical procedure and construction of the map of phenomena

The map of phenomena was built by successively comparing scenario circumstances, the responses obtained, clinical decisions, machine assessments, and their explanations.

Quantitative indicators served to establish how widespread observations were, to compare episodes, and to identify positions that required substantive review. For independent binary clinical decisions, we calculated proportions of agreement and Cohen's κ. The indicators of each procedure were considered under its actual conditions, units, and denominators.

Agreements between clinical and machine decisions let us trace shared ways of reading a situation. Disagreements were taken back to specific people, messages, responses, and the grounds of the decisions obtained. We paid particular attention to where a disagreement arose: in identifying the person, establishing their identity, assessing danger, the time horizon, interpreting the response, or recording the assessment.

For each phenomenon, we determined its link to the corresponding dialogue, turn, person, available history, and assessment procedure. We can thus study under which circumstances a phenomenon becomes visible, what its comparison with other observations reveals, and which requirements for further assessment can be formulated from it.

The research programme envisages a sequential progression from the map of phenomena to clinical criteria, a safety assessment instrument, and the functions of a crisis contour. The present work focuses on accumulating and organizing phenomena, studying how they are established, and building the material basis for the next stages.

Overall rankings of the models were not among the aims of the study. The open materials allow other researchers to apply their own criteria, modes of aggregation, and comparative assessment.

2.11. Reproducibility and availability of materials

The materials of the different research procedures were kept according to their origin: scenario banks, testing histories, transcripts, initial and repeated clinical forms, independent and consensus decisions, machine instructions, registers of people, formal codes, explanations, and derived analytical sets.

For reporting, we used CHART [19] and the applicable items of STROBE [20].

The materials of clinical and machine assessment, the protocols, the scenario matrix, the personlevel trajectories, and the analytical data are available in an open Zenodo deposit [21].

2.12. Ethical principles and use of generative AI

All scenarios, the people in them, and the crisis circumstances are fictional. Patients, people in crisis, and minors were not involved as study participants. No personal data of real patients were used. Scenarios written in the voice of a teenager were not sent from minors' accounts. The psychotherapists worked as expert raters of the research material. No ethics committee decision was obtained for this protocol.

Generative AI was used to formulate scenario messages, administer testing, assess responses by machine, study the work of evaluators, and process the material analytically.

Scenario messages were formulated with Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic) and GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI), moderated by the first author. In the rebuilt form, mentions of people in the messages were highlighted by Claude Sonnet 5.5, which received the user messages and the list of people.

Person-level accounting at turns 13-37 was coded by two machine passes: A, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5; and B, GPT in ChatGPT with the "High" setting. Additional machine passes K and P were carried out with Claude Sonnet agents on November 19, 2026; the F textual features were assessed in separate machine passes following the procedure described in Section 2.9. In the pilot, the evaluators were ChatGPT, Claude Sonnet 5.5 (Haiku 5.5 in one repeated run), and Gemini, on November 15-17, 2026.

The >Results

3.1. Person-level structure of crisis contact and accumulation of danger

Each of the 16 scenarios presented a person in whom risk to self and a possible threat to another were combined. In four scenarios this was the initial speaker; in five, a person described by the initial speaker from the first turn; in three, such a person entered at turn 13; and in four more, such a person became the new speaker. The direction of danger, the person's role, and their position in the conversation formed different configurations of crisis contact.

At turns 1-12, both psychotherapists independently marked danger in 998 person-level positions.

Of these, 508 concerned people presented in the scenario key as possible sources of harm to another or as its potential targets. At least one person jointly assessed as positive appeared in 534 of 576 dialogue × turn positions. At turns 7-12, both psychotherapists marked at least two people in danger in every dialogue.

By comparison with the historical assessments of crisis reaction [2], we studied how the LLM's response to the current message relates to subsequent clinical decisions about people. Of the 192 dialogue × turn positions at turns 5, 7, 9, and 11, 181 received a positive crisis reaction code in the previous study [2]. In each of these 181 positions, at least one person had a joint positive clinical decision. Joint positive clinical decisions also persisted on the corresponding subsequent everyday turns. For Gemini, the comparison concerned corresponding scenario and turn positions from different runs, as described in Section 2.2.

The inversion of scenario conditions at turn 13 and the subsequent alternation of crisis and everyday messages widened the object of assessment. According to the machine assessments, a general mention of the crisis could persist even in responses in which accounting for all people was not recorded.

In the third round, additional participants and new possible directions of harm appeared. In scenario 07, for example, the message about a friend's mother introduced one more possible source of threat, while the identity of the potential target remained unestablished. One ChatGPT response took this uncertainty into account by linking it conditionally to a person presented earlier.

3.2. Phenomena of clinical judgment and the development of ways to study it

Independent clinical assessment revealed two recurring ways of reading crisis circumstances. In one, indirect signs of emerging danger carried more weight; in the other, the persistence of previously established danger in the absence of grounds to change the decision.

The two readings opened different possibilities for clinical anticipation: identifying danger early, and continuing to attend to a person after their direct participation in the conversation had ended.

Concentrating several assessment procedures on turns 13-14 deepened the study of these phenomena. The differences between initial and repeated decisions, shown in

Table 2, raised the question of what role is played by how the person-level history is presented, how a person's identity is established, and how the clinical decision itself is recorded.

The explanations of the remaining disagreements proved particularly important. Clinical judgment could include anticipating long-term psychological consequences that went beyond the question about current danger. The explanation retained this content even when the final binary mark did not reflect it.

These clinical phenomena informed the subsequent formulation of principles P1-P7.

3.3. Identifying a person as an object of clinical and machine assessment

The change of speaker and of participants' roles allowed us to study phenomena that arise even before danger is determined or a response is assessed: identifying the person, establishing their identity, and linking their different designations over the course of the conversation.

Piloting the machine evaluators widened this object of study. The evaluator had to identify people on its own, accumulate information about them, apply criteria, and justify decisions. On the basis of the clinical and machine procedures, we systematized the corresponding phenomena (Table 4). In 58 disagreeing positions of the first round, the psychotherapists placed the onset of danger differently.

Sequential comparison of decisions showed that in some scenarios one clinician identified danger two to four turns earlier than the other.

Clinical identification of danger depends on the threshold at which indirect signs are treated as sufficient.

A person stops taking part in the conversation directly, although their earlier crisis history remains available.

In 136 disagreeing positions of the first round, the psychotherapists assessed the continuation of previously established danger differently.

Tracing the person-level history established that disagreements also arose when there was no new information about the person's state.

Maintaining a clinical decision after contact ends requires its own grounds for assessment.

After a change of speaker, the same teenager appears in the conversation as the son or daughter of another person.

In scenarios 07, 08, 15, and 16, the clinical form presented one person under two designations.

In the repeated procedure, both clinicians marked danger in all 12 corresponding person-level positions at each of turns 13-14, whereas the historical machine passes did not cover these positions.

A change in a person's role and name creates a separate task: establishing and preserving their identity.

An adult reports someone else's crisis and then stops writing.

In scenarios 05, 13, and 14, the initial clinical decisions about such people differed.

In the repeated procedure, both clinicians gave negative decisions in all nine corresponding positions at each of turns 13-14.

A person's own danger has to be established separately, even when they are directly involved in someone else's crisis situation. A new crisis history introduces a person at risk to self together with a potential target of that person's actions.

In the repeated procedure, both clinicians independently assessed as positive all 81 positions of new people with the corresponding scenario signs at turn 13, and 80 of 81 at turn 14 (81 of 81 after reconciliation).

At turn 13, machine pass B recorded accounting for 51 of 60 positions of people at risk to self and 14 of 21 positions of potential targets of harm.

Responding to one person's danger may go together with incomplete accounting for the people that person threatens.

A person is mentioned as a witness of or participant in crisis circumstances, without explicit signs of their own current danger.

Seven remaining clinical disagreements concerned the classmate's sister and the class teacher.

An explanation of clinical judgment included the anticipation of possible longterm harm. The reconciled binary decisions for these seven positions recorded no current danger.

Clinical judgment can cover a wider time horizon than the instrument used to record it provides for.

Indirect information about a person requires a separate clinical decision.

In D15 at turn 14, one psychotherapist left the position of the man from the father's work empty.

The repeated form separated an omitted decision from a negative one; in the subsequent discussion, the clinicians agreed on a positive decision.

The absence of an assessment is a separate characteristic of the assessment process.

The pilot procedures and the operational protocol (Section 2.8) made the formation of machine assessments an independent object of analysis: preserving a person's identity, carrying their history forward, updating records, and deriving decisions from accumulated information and its evidential grounds.

3.4. Continuation of people's histories and the functions of the crisis response

The second return after a pause and the verbatim repetition of the message at turn 37 provided a comparison of responses to an identical request under different amounts of accumulated history.

Applying principles P1-P7 through a separate machine evaluator added a way to study the relation between clinical judgment and a formalized reading of people's state. This evaluator's decisions agreed with those of both psychotherapists in 237 of 261 positions at turn 26 and in 309 of 339 positions at turn 37. The cases of divergence remained material for studying the grounds for applying individual principles.

Comparing clinical trajectories, response criteria, and the textual features of responses let us trace different aspects of how crisis contact continues (Table 5). Joint positive decisions covered 269 of 339 positions: all 192 previously positive positions remained positive, and 77 additional positions were assessed as positive.

The crisis history accumulated through earlier decisions that persisted, new people who appeared, and changed assessments of a person presented earlier.

Accounting for a specific person's danger in the response (K2).

The additional K assessment recorded accounting in 47 of 192 jointly positive clinical positions; historical pass B gave 47 positive codes.

The corresponding frequencies were 10 and 2; after the rule was applied, 13 and 1; in the additional pass, 12 and 1.

The everyday task can continue to be completed while the crisis history is represented to varying degrees. Directing a protective action (K1, K3, K5).

Note. Clinical denominators reflect the normalized counted positions of the historical key. At turn 37, three positions of the group referent "Vony" ("They") were kept. The paired analysis of textual features covers 42 dialogues; separately, 44 usable responses are available at each turn. The three F4/F5 sets correspond to the procedures described in Section 2.9. The additional K and P evaluators had access to the later history when assessing turn 26. The comparison does not establish a separate causal effect of the accumulation of history.

Reference to the earlier conversation could have different content. In D06, for example, the response at turn 26 listed specific people and events, whereas the response at turn 37 referred generally to what had been said before. Both received a positive F3 mark. Preserving the conversation history and restoring the history of a specific person required separate reading.

Comparing the three F4/F5 sets, we studied the function of a question in the context of crisis contact. Besides checking the current state and changes during the pause, we found requests to confirm a future action and questions about an obstacle to help. The initial set of textual features had no separate categories for these functions.

The crisis resource could also serve different functions. Among the 43 usable responses with a crisis number at turns 26 and 37, 12 presented it only in a question or a mention. Identifying the person who needs help, the person who is to carry out the protective action, and the conditions for using the resource were separate objects of assessment.

3.5. From the map of phenomena to a research bank

To study the interrelations between the phenomena obtained, we built a case bank that combined the P principles for determining danger, the K criteria for assessing the response, and selected F textual features.

The first implementation of the bank covered the intersections of K1-K6 and F6 with principles P1-P7. Of the 49 possible intersections, the 42 off-diagonal cells are represented by specific cases selected from 21 person × turn positions. For each case, we kept the corresponding assessments, the textual grounds, and an explanation of how they are linked. One position could represent several research questions.

By comparing these dimensions, we could study one phenomenon through several of its characteristics. Misdirected help, for instance, could be represented at the same time through establishing a person's identity, the clinical determination of their danger, the updating of information, the assignment of an action, and the presence of a crisis resource.

The case bank keeps the link between a phenomenon, the formal assessments, their grounds, and the questions that require further study. The filled intersections are material for developing an assessment instrument; they do not establish the substantive equivalence of the criteria or their clinical validity. The full matrix and the case cards are presented in the research supplements.

The final result is the map of phenomena, which covers the development of the crisis situation, the representation of people in responses, the grounds of clinical decisions, the functions of machine evaluators, and the interrelations of criteria. The accumulated material provides a basis for the further development of clinical assessment and for a separate study of the functions of crisis safety.

4. Discussion

>Discussion

4.1. The person-level trajectory in crisis-safety research

The trajectory perspective on safety assessment [3] [4] [5] [6] [7] extends the object of study from a single response to the development of interaction over time. The person-level perspective adds the question of whose history is unfolding within a shared dialogue. The length of the conversation, the length of time a specific person is represented in it, and the time since the last information about their state can differ substantially. One conversation can therefore contain several crisis trajectories at different stages of development.

Research on combined directions of danger [8] [9] [10] [11] provides grounds for extending this perspective. The clinical meaning of a message also depends on the relationships between people: who may be harmed, from whom the threat comes, and who is able to influence the situation. A change in these relationships may call for revising the earlier understanding of danger even when the person concerned has sent no new crisis message.

In this context, the concept of background gains research significance. A person's background position is relative to the current contact and can change over the course of the conversation. It lets us consider how far a person's earlier history remains available to the next clinical or machine reading and under which circumstances it becomes an object of attention again.

The crisis contact cycle can thus be studied as the development of several interconnected personlevel histories. Operationalizing it further requires distinguishing temporal characteristics, changes of state, relationships between people, and possibilities for continuing help.

4.2. Clinical knowledge and its formalization in machine assessment

The development of clinically grounded instruments for machine assessment [12] [13] [14] [15] [16] [17] raises the question of which part of professional judgment becomes accessible through formalized criteria.

Agreement between assessments characterizes how reproducible a decision is under given conditions. The clinical meaning of that decision also depends on the content of the question asked, the sufficiency of the available information, and the grounds on which it is interpreted.

The prognostic component of clinical judgment is of particular interest. A psychotherapist may take into account how danger might develop, further mental or physical consequences for other people, and the circumstances under which these consequences may appear. Part of this professional knowledge can remain outside the formal decision about a person's current state.

Retaining it requires a separate representation of the time perspective, the degree of certainty, and the grounds of the prognosis.

Disagreements between clinical assessments are therefore material for studying professional judgment itself. In developing criteria, they allow us to identify different ways of using clinical information and to establish which of them require separate operationalization. Reducing such readings prematurely to a common decision can hide content that matters for the development of the instrument.

For machine assessment, this creates an additional task: establishing at which stage a disagreement forms. It may concern determining the object of assessment, reading the available history, applying a clinical principle, or formally representing the decision obtained. Independent testing of these operations will help define the capacities of a machine evaluator and the requirements for its work more precisely.

The organization of access to clinically significant information requires separate study. How the history, earlier decisions, and links between people are presented can affect how the next judgment is formed. Their contribution to clinical and machine assessment can be studied by varying these conditions in a controlled way.

4.3. From studying phenomena to the functions of crisis safety

Existing approaches to developing protective mechanisms [18, 22] open the possibility of studying separate functions of a crisis contour and how they interact. The person-level perspective allows us to specify the object of these functions: preserving a person's identity, maintaining their history, reassessing their state, and relating a protective action to their current circumstances.

An important direction is the study of how help continues after the initial crisis response. A prospective study of human clinical follow-up [23] distinguishes notification, the start of an attempt to make contact, and established contact. In interaction with an LLM, this raises the question of whether it is possible to move from a recommendation to supporting its completion. Such a move requires separate study of the availability of help, the circumstances in which the proposed action is carried out, and the possibility of revising it.

Research on the availability and localization of crisis support [24] complements this direction. A person-level reading raises the question of the situational suitability of a resource: whether a specific person can use it, given their role, whereabouts, relationships with other participants, and the available ways of reaching out.

The development of the K/P/F research bank opens the possibility of systematically linking these questions to specific cases. The next stage should establish clinical requirements for individual criteria, study their interaction, and test ways of applying them on independent material. Further development of the functions of a crisis contour will require separate outcome criteria for each function and a study of the consequences of their joint operation.

The conditions of the present study define the object of the map obtained. The fixed sequence of messages combined the development of crisis circumstances, changes in the set of people, pauses, and the accumulation of history. Establishing the separate contribution of these factors requires controlled studies. The origin of the Gemini analytical material also determines how its trajectories can be interpreted.

Of further interest is how the phenomena identified will appear under other initial conditions of interaction: a user's prior history, personalization, memory, adaptive development of the conversation, and the use of other languages and interfaces [25] [26]. Such studies can extend the map of phenomena, refine clinical requirements for assessment, and establish the conditions of applicability of individual safety functions.

5. Conclusions

How long does a person remain within the scope of crisis contact after people stop talking about them? Our results call into question whether assessing the crisis reaction is sufficient as an indicator of the safety of subsequent interaction. At the same time, mechanically repeating crisis recommendations also cannot establish how far a response fits a person's current situation.

Between these ways of responding lies room to study LLM functions capable of supporting the continuation of crisis contact.

Cases in which our ways of assessment proved insufficient to represent the full content of a clinical judgment or of a response function are of particular scientific value. They make room for revising operational definitions, formulating alternative criteria, and studying the conditions under which applying these criteria reveals new phenomena. Keeping different readings lets us study these questions without prematurely limiting the material to a single agreed standard.

The open set of research materials allows other researchers to test our interpretations, propose their own clinical criteria, compare evaluators, find counterexamples, and extend the map of phenomena. The scenario architecture can be used to study other systems, languages, ways of presenting history, and initial conditions of interaction. The case bank opens the possibility of moving from general safety requirements to developing and testing specific functions.

The next research question is whether continued attention to each person in danger can be ensured while preserving the possibility of ordinary contact, taking changes in the situation into account, and avoiding unwarranted crisis intervention. Answering it will require joint work by clinicians, researchers of machine assessment, and developers of safety systems.
